Ancile Official Release

Ancile is a command line tool that attempts to block all Windows spying and unwanted upgrades.

Latest Version

v1.10 (2016-02-26)

 

Features

  • Sync Windows time with ntp.org
  • Block unwanted hosts using the Windows hosts file, routing table, and firewall
  • Change windows update to check/notify (do not download/install) or disable it entirely
  • Disable automatic delivery of Internet explorer via windows update
  • Disable CEIP/GWX/SkyDrive(aka OneDrive)/SpyNet/Telemetry/WiFi Sense
  • Disable remote registry
  • Disable unwanted scheduled tasks
  • Disable unwanted services
  • Disable the Windows 10 forced update
  • Remove Microsoft's diagnostics tracking
  • Hide/Uninstall unwanted Windows updates
  • Add 3rd party plugins

 

Instructions

Ancile does not require installation and can be run directly from within it's parent folder.

  1. Download the latest version (https://bitbucket.org/ancile_development/ancile/downloads/)
  2. Unzip the archive
  3. Navigate to the Ancile directory
  4. Edit "config.ini" to make any custom changes (optional)
  5. Right click on "ancile.cmd"
  6. Select "Run as Administrator" from the menu
  7. Follow the on screen instructions

 

Build your own release

Ancile allows you to build your own release and customize it to your needs.

  1. Clone the latest version of Ancile Build tools (git clone https://matthewlinton@bitbucket.org/ancile_development/ancile.git)).
  2. Navigate to the Ancile directory
  3. Read through the "README.md" file for instructions on how to modify and build Ancile.

I strongly suspect you did a copy/paste of a command you didn't fully research and understand. We've all been there ;) That said I think you've done a great job with Ancile. Here's the fix.

We're going to use the terms 'admin privileges' and 'admin rights' as synonyms here, but we should keep in mind the difference between an admin account with admin rights and an elevated account, a.k.a. a non-admin account with admin privileges.

On line 80 of 'ancile.cmd' you invoke <net session> with:

net session >nul 2>&1

then redirecting the STDERR 2 to STDERR 1, executing the rest of the script only if the ERRORLEVEL is 0, i.e. no errors are thrown, or sending it to ERRORCHECK otherwise - lines 82-88.

net session standard errors handling is based on whether the Windows Service "Server" is running when the <net session> command is invoked, regardless of the privileges granted to the user executing it. Testing the command(1): 

net session >nul & ECHO %ERRORLEVEL%

on an Administrator account in a Command Prompt with admin rights and without admin rights, leads to unpredictable STDERR results:

<----------------------------------------------> ADMINISTRATOR ACCOUNT
-\ | with | with |
- \ | "Server" service | "Server" service |
- \ | running | not started |
------------------------------------------------
with | | |
admin | 0 | 2 |
priv | | |
------------------------------------------------
without| | |
admin | 2 | 2 |
priv | | |
------------------------------------------------

You can clearly see the issues. If the "Server" service has not been started, you're halting the execution of the script even if invoked as admin with admin rights - STDERR 2. Only while "Server" is running, the <net session> behaves as you may expect. I've done the same testing on an elevated account and not surprisingly, the results are identical.

 

The fix is quite straightforward: you need to check the "Server" service status before calling the <net session> command, and go from there. You could use net start(2), but I suggest using the sc query command, it looks more effective:

sc query LanmanServer | findstr "RUNNING" >nul
IF %ERRORLEVEL% NEQ 0 (
 ECHO PRIV CHECK FAIL: The LanmanServer service is not running. <net session> fails.>> "%LOGFILE%"
 whoami /all >> "%LOGFILE%" 2>&1
 ECHO FATAL ERROR: The Server service is not running. 
 ECHO Run services.msc and start it manually. 
 ECHO Then execute ancile.cmd again.
 ECHO.
 GOTO END
)

At this point we would want to start the "Server" service with <sc start>, but you need admin priv. I don't think that leaving the task to the user is such a bad idea anyway.

On finding a better method to check for current user privileges, here's my take:

@ECHO OFF
REM .
REM Checking if the user is a member of the local administrator' group, i.e. if it's an admin account
REM .
SET admin=N
SET domain=%USERDOMAIN%\
IF /i "%domain%" EQU "%computername%\" SET domain=
SET user=%domain%%username%
FOR /f "Tokens=*" %%a IN ('net localgroup administrators^| find /i "%user%"') DO ( SET admin=Y )

REM .
REM Checking if the user has administrative rights.
REM .
SET priv=Y
FOR /f "Tokens=*" %%a IN ('attrib +A %systemroot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts^| find /i "Access denied"') DO ( SET priv=N )

IF %priv% EQU Y ( GOTO WITHPRIV ) ELSE ( GOTO WITHOUTPRIV )

:WITHOUTPRIV
IF %admin% EQU Y ( ECHO admin without privileges ) ELSE ( ECHO non-elevated account )
GOTO FATALERROR

:WITHPRIV
IF %admin% EQU Y ( ECHO admin with privileges ) ELSE ( ECHO user with privileges )


:FATALERROR

A brief explanation on why the use of the ATTRIB command which at first glance appears crude and invasive, turns out to be innocuous. ATTRIB switch on and off the attributes of the files, but the only one we are using is the 'A' attribute that stands for "Archive". The 'A' attribute goes back to the days of MS-DOS and it was created with the intention of marking the files that were changed since the last time they were backed up. It's nothing, but a flag and it has no direct impact on the OS if changed. The practical usage of it came with the command XCOPY which was archive attributes aware, hence it could have been manipulating files with the 'A' attribute set. Most files today have the 'A' attribute set, because most files aren't only accessed, but also modified. The 'hosts' file in System32\drivers\etc is no exception. 

Therefore by setting the 'Archive' attribute on 'hosts' we are doing a great job of absolutely and precisely nothing. And even if 'hosts' was ever only been accessed, setting the 'A' attribute on it would make no difference whatsoever. And yet the user needs to have administrative rights to be allowed to.

 

It seems to me a rough unprofessional no-nonsense clean hack to get the job done. I'm not loving it, but it is the best solution I could came up with at the moment, which doesn't seem to have been thought yet. While the idea of calling a command that knowingly requires administrative rights to be executed, intending to manipulate its output, is what <net session> has been used for. On this lines you could use the command:

OPENFILES >nul 2>nul

suppressing anything, but ERRORLEVEL 1 which would be thrown if you don't have admin rights. But where is the fun in that? ;) You judge, but the fact remains: my solution is an ubiquitous way to check for privileges from Windows NT on as all the commands I'm using where introduced with MD-DOS.
